facts.name: Crocus
facts.latin: Crocus vernus and other spring crocus
facts.color: Purple, white, yellow or striped cups
facts.light: Full sun to part shade; fine under trees that leaf out after it blooms
facts.notes: One of the first flowers of spring, often up through the last snow. Plant the corms 3 to 4 inches deep in fall, in groups of 10 or more. The grassy leaves fade by early summer. Squirrels and chipmunks dig up newly planted corms; chicken wire over the planting stops them.
facts.toxSrc: ASPCA: spring crocus can cause vomiting, diarrhea and drooling in dogs and cats (autumn crocus, a different plant, is far more toxic)

sources.title: English Gardens (Metro Detroit garden centers): Flower Record Crocus
sources.note: Sold at English Gardens, with 'Jeanne D'Arc' (white), 'Golden Yellow' and 'Blue Pearl' crocus; 3 to 4 in tall, hardy to zone 3.

sources.title: MSU Extension: Where are my bulbs? Why aren't they flowering?
sources.note: Plant crocus, snowdrops, squill and other small bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep.

sources.title: Extension (Wildlife Damage Management): Squirrels digging up crocus, hyacinth and tulip bulbs
sources.note: Wire baskets, chicken wire or hardware cloth over newly planted crocus corms keep squirrels from digging them up.

sources.title: ASPCA: Keep Your Pet Safe While You Enjoy Springtime Gardening
sources.note: Spring crocus can cause vomiting, diarrhea and drooling; autumn crocus (Colchicum) is a different, more dangerous plant.

companions.why: Hellebores bloom in late winter and early spring, and their flowers and leaves pair well with crocus.
Early daffodils add height and more color to a bed of spring crocus.
